hook: Studied by Irene Pepperberg from 1977 to 2007 at Brandeis; Alex learned over 100 words and used 'none' to indicate zero — the first non-human animal documented to grasp the concept of nothingness as a number.

In a 2002 Oxford study by Alex Kacelnik's group, captive crow Betty spontaneously bent a straight piece of wire into a hook to retrieve a food bucket from a vertical tube — a behavior never observed in her wild conspecifics.

In a 2006 Bronx Zoo study by Joshua Plotnik, Frans de Waal, and Diana Reiss, Happy repeatedly touched a white X painted above her eye while looking in a wall-mounted mirror — the first elephant to pass the mark test.
In April 2016, Inky squeezed out of an unsecured tank at the National Aquarium of New Zealand in Napier, crossed the floor, and slid down a 150mm drainpipe back to the sea.

In 2016 at Royal Burgers' Zoo Arnhem, dying matriarch Mama recognized retired primatologist Jan van Hooff after years apart, embraced him, and patted his head — the encounter filmed and described in his 2019 Mama's Last Hug.

Nicola Clayton's Cambridge studies (1998–2007) showed scrub jays remember what they cached, where, and when — re-caching perishable worms before they spoil. First experimental demonstration of episodic-like memory in a non-human.

In Helmut Prior's 2008 Goethe University study, magpies with a yellow sticker placed below their throat repeatedly tried to remove it only when given access to a mirror — the first non-mammal to pass the mark test.

subject_name: karl von frisch bee waggle dance
hook: In experiments from the 1920s to 1960s in Brunnwinkl, Austria, Karl von Frisch decoded the honey bee waggle dance — direction relative to the sun, duration encoding distance — earning the 1973 Nobel Prize for what is still the only known symbolic communication system in an invertebrate.

Raised from 1966 by Allen and Beatrix Gardner at the University of Nevada, Washoe acquired roughly 350 ASL signs and once signed 'water bird' on seeing a swan — though the productivity of such combinations remains debated.

At the Language Research Center in Atlanta, Sue Savage-Rumbaugh documented Kanzi learning lexigrams by observation from infancy in the 1980s; he reliably responds to novel spoken English sentences such as 'put the keys in the refrigerator'.

In Sally Boysen's 1989–1996 Ohio State studies, the chimp Sheba learned to associate Arabic numerals 0–4 with quantities and to sum hidden caches — performing reliably above chance once she could point to the symbol rather than the larger pile.

At Kyoto University's Primate Research Institute, Tetsuro Matsuzawa's chimp Ai has used numerals 1–9 since the 1980s; her son Ayumu later outperformed human adults on briefly flashed numeral sequences in a 2007 working-memory study.

Russell Balda and Alan Kamil's field and lab studies from the 1980s showed Clark's nutcrackers recover thousands of pine-seed caches scattered across kilometres of Rocky Mountain terrain months later — geometric memory tied to landmark configurations.

Field studies by Gavin Hunt in 1996 documented wild New Caledonian crows manufacturing two distinct tool types from Pandanus leaves — stepped and tapered — with regional variation suggesting cultural transmission.
In a 2014 Auckland study by Alex Taylor's group, the crow nicknamed 007 solved an eight-step puzzle box on first exposure, sequencing previously learned sub-tasks to reach a piece of meat.

In a 2001 New York Aquarium study by Diana Reiss and Lori Marino, bottlenose dolphins Presley and Tab oriented to body marks visible only in a mirror — the first marine mammal to pass a version of the mark test.

In Joshua Plotnik's 2011 Thai Elephant Conservation Center study, paired elephants learned to pull both ends of a rope simultaneously to drag a baited tray — and to wait for an absent partner before pulling, indicating they understood the partner's role.

Gerald Wilkinson's 1984 Costa Rica field studies showed common vampire bats regurgitate blood meals to roost-mates who failed to feed — preferentially to relatives but also to reciprocating non-kin, an early documented case of non-human reciprocal altruism.

Con Slobodchikoff's 1990s–2000s Northern Arizona University recordings show Gunnison's prairie dogs use distinct alarm calls encoding predator type, size, and colour — different calls for a tall thin human in a yellow shirt versus a short stocky one in blue.

Tom Flower's 2014 Kalahari field study documented fork-tailed drongos giving false alarm calls — including mimicked calls of other species — to scare meerkats and pied babblers off their food, varying the call type to defeat habituation.

In a 2007 Masai Mara study by Jakob Bro-Jørgensen, male topi antelopes gave false predator alarm snorts as oestrous females tried to leave their territory — keeping them inside long enough to mate again.

In Alex Schnell and Nicola Clayton's 2021 marshmallow-test analogue, common cuttlefish waited up to two minutes for a preferred prawn rather than eat an available shrimp — performance correlating with their later learning scores.

Jennifer Mather and Roland Anderson's 1990s Seattle Aquarium studies documented common octopuses learning to unscrew jar lids to extract crabs — manipulating the lid with multiple arms while bracing the jar with others.

In a 2009 Indonesian field study by Julian Finn and colleagues, veined octopuses were filmed collecting and carrying coconut-shell halves across the seafloor for later use as portable shelters — the first documented invertebrate tool use.

Steven Reppert's 2003 Massachusetts studies decoded the monarch butterfly's time-compensated sun compass — a circadian clock in the antennae, not the brain, that lets a single multi-generation migration reach the same Mexican oyamel groves each November.

Cordula Mora and colleagues' 2004 Auckland study showed homing pigeons detect magnetic field anomalies through receptors in the upper beak — disrupting the trigeminal nerve abolished their ability to discriminate magnetic stimuli.

In Matthias Wittlinger, Rüdiger Wehner, and Harald Wolf's 2006 Tunisian field experiments, lengthening Saharan desert ants' legs with stilts made them overshoot the nest — proving they count steps to integrate distance on featureless salt-pan terrain.

In Olli Loukola, Lars Chittka, and colleagues' 2017 Queen Mary London study, buff-tailed bumblebees learned to roll a small ball into a target to obtain sugar water — and naive observer bees learned the trick faster from a demonstrator than from a moving magnet.

At the University of Vienna's Goffin Lab, Alice Auersperg's 2013 study filmed the cockatoo Pipin sequentially undoing five different locks — bolt, screw, wheel, latch, key — to open a transparent box, with the order learned from scratch.
In Mathias Osvath and Can Kabadayi's 2017 Lund University study, ravens chose and saved a tool to be used 17 hours later for a food puzzle — outperforming great apes on the same future-planning task.

Nicola Clayton's 2001 Cambridge studies showed Western scrub jays re-cache food in private after being observed by a conspecific — but only individuals who had themselves stolen another's cache, suggesting they project their own experience onto others.

Kaeli Swift and John Marzluff's 2015 Seattle study documented common ravens and American crows gathering around dead conspecifics, scolding, and avoiding the location for days — interpreted as danger-learning rather than mourning, but the behavior is consistent and ritualized.

Karen McComb and Lucy Baker's 2005 Amboseli study showed African elephants spend significantly more time investigating elephant skulls and ivory than buffalo or rhino bones, returning to known individuals' remains — described carefully as 'unusual response', not mourning.

Jan van Hooff's 1972 ethogram and Marina Davila-Ross's 2009 University of Portsmouth playback studies established the 'play face' — a relaxed open-mouth expression with vocalizations — as a homologue of human laughter conserved across the great apes.

Jaak Panksepp and Jeff Burgdorf's 1998–2003 Bowling Green studies recorded 50 kHz ultrasonic 'chirps' from young rats when tickled on the nape — the rats sought out the experimenter's hand and approached locations where tickling had occurred.

Raoul Schwing's 2013 University of Vienna observations and earlier Routledge field reports document keas in the New Zealand Southern Alps repeatedly sliding down snowbanks on their backs and dropped objects — long-duration object and locomotor play with no immediate function.

Herbert Terrace's 1970s Columbia project taught Nim Chimpsky 125 signs, then concluded the chimp was responding to trainer cues rather than constructing language — the 1979 paper that recalibrated how the field interprets ape-language studies.

Sue Carter and Larry Young's 1990s–2000s studies of prairie voles linked pair bonding and biparental care to oxytocin and vasopressin receptor distribution — distinguishing them from the closely related, non-monogamous meadow vole.

In Masanori Kohda's 2019 Osaka City study, cleaner wrasses repeatedly scraped a coloured throat mark against substrates while in front of a mirror — the first fish reported to pass a version of the mark test, though the criteria are actively debated.

In a 2016 Atlantis Bahamas study by Csilla Ari and Dominic D'Agostino, giant manta rays in front of a mirror increased frequency of contingency-checking movements and unusual self-directed behaviors — suggestive but not yet diagnostic of mirror self-recognition.

Sanjeeta Sharma Pokharel and colleagues' 2022 study in northern Bengal documented Asian elephants carrying dead calves in their trunks for hours to days and visiting carcasses repeatedly — five separate cases compiled from forest department records.

Three to five generations separate the monarchs that leave central Mexico in spring from those that return in autumn — yet the returning butterflies, never having flown the route, find the same dozen oyamel groves each year via the antennal sun compass.

Rüdiger Wehner's 1970s–1990s Zurich field work showed Saharan desert ants navigate using the polarization pattern of skylight detected by a specialized dorsal rim region of the compound eye — vector integration combined with the step-counting pedometer.

Field observations from Monterey Bay onward — formalized in Katherine Ralls's 1995 studies and subsequent Monterey Bay Aquarium ethograms — document sea otters using a stone anvil rested on the chest while floating, striking shellfish against it repeatedly to crack the shell.

At Fazenda Boa Vista in Brazil, Dorothy Fragaszy and Elisabetta Visalberghi's 2004–2010 field studies documented wild bearded capuchins selecting hammer stones and anvil stones to crack palm nuts — choosing stones for weight, with juveniles refining technique over years.

In Jorg Massen's 2020 University of Vienna study, common ravens learned a two-rope cooperation task — both birds had to pull simultaneously — and refused to cooperate with partners who had previously cheated them out of the reward.

Frans Plooij's 1978 Gombe observations and later Richard Byrne's 1990s compendium document juvenile chimps misdirecting adults' attention with feigned alarm or false grooming invitations to monopolize food — case-by-case but consistent across long-term field sites.

Russ Balda and Alan Kamil's 1996 Northern Arizona study showed Clark's nutcrackers find caches using the geometric midpoint between two landmarks — interpolating a buried seed's location even when both landmarks are moved as a pair.

Alex Thornton and Katherine McAuliffe's 2006 Uganda study of banded mongooses showed adults bring live but disabled scorpions and beetles to pups, scaling prey difficulty to pup age — one of the clearest documented cases of teaching in a non-human mammal.

Oskar Pfungst's 1907 Berlin investigation showed the horse Hans was not doing arithmetic — he was reading unconscious postural cues from his trainer Wilhelm von Osten. The methodological lesson reshaped animal cognition: control for inadvertent cuing or your finding is worthless.

John Pilley (Wofford College) trained border collie Chaser from 2004, documenting that she reliably identified 1,022 named objects by noun — the largest tested vocabulary of any non-human animal — and could also use fast-mapping exclusion to acquire a new word after a single exposure.

In a 2004 Science paper by Juliane Kaminski, Josep Call, and Julia Fischer at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, border collie Rico demonstrated fast-mapping: he chose a novel, unnamed object from a set of familiar ones, and retained the new word four weeks after a single exposure — mirroring a key step in human language acquisition.

Alexandra Horowitz (Barnard College, Behavioural Processes, 2009) showed that the canine 'guilty look' correlates with owner scolding, not actual transgression: innocent dogs scolded by misinformed owners showed the most exaggerated guilt displays, revealing the look is a submission response to cues, not evidence of moral self-awareness.

subject_name: african wild dog sneeze voting walker 2017
hook: Reena Walker (Brown University) and colleagues (Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2017) analysed 68 social rallies in five Botswana packs and found sneezes function as quorum votes: ~10 sneezes triggered a group hunt without the dominant pair, but only ~3 sufficed when dominants were involved — the first recorded sneeze-based democratic decision in any animal.

Brian Hare and Michael Tomasello (Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, Science, 2002) showed that dogs outperform chimpanzees and socialized wolves at following human pointing and gaze to locate hidden food, and that even minimally socialised puppies succeed — implying social-cognitive skills for reading human communicative intent evolved during domestication.

P.E. Stander (Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology, 1992) analysed 486 coordinated lion hunts in Namibia and found individual lionesses consistently occupied the same positional role — 'wings' flushing prey, 'centres' making the kill — and that hunts succeeded more often when lionesses held their preferred positions, demonstrating persistent role specialisation in a wild feline.

In a 2021 Cambridge study led by Alex Schnell, common cuttlefish (Sepia officinalis) waited up to 130 seconds for a preferred prey item rather than taking an immediately available inferior one — tolerating delays comparable to chimpanzees and parrots — and those that waited longest also scored best on a separate learning task, the first time self-control has been linked to intelligence in a non-human outside great apes.

In a 2021 study by Alexandra Schnell's team at Cambridge and the Marine Biological Laboratory, Sepia officinalis reliably remembered what food was available, at which marked location, and how long ago — and this episodic-like memory remained sharp right into old age, unlike episodic memory in aging humans.

In a 2012 Macquarie University study led by Culum Brown, male mourning cuttlefish (Sepia plangon) simultaneously displayed male courtship coloration on the side facing a female and female body patterns on the side facing a rival male — in 39% of trials when a rival was present — preventing interference while courting, a case of concurrent tactical deception toward two individuals.

subject_name: veined octopus coconut shell tool use
hook: In a 2009 Current Biology paper by Julian Finn and Mark Norman of Museum Victoria, veined octopuses (Amphioctopus marginatus) filmed off Bali and Sulawesi collected discarded coconut-shell halves, carried them awkwardly under their bodies across open sand, then later assembled two halves into a spherical shelter — the first documented case of tool use in an invertebrate requiring transport and future deployment of an object.

Field observations and a 2001 report by Norman, Finn, and Tregenza documented that Thaumoctopus mimicus off North Sulawesi deploys its sea-snake impersonation — trailing two arms while burying the rest — specifically and exclusively when harassed by damselfish, a known prey of sea snakes, rather than applying it to all threats, implying context-dependent selection of mimicry target.

In experiments published by Robert Jackson (University of Canterbury) across the 1990s and confirmed by Fiona Cross and Jackson in a 2019 Journal of Experimental Biology paper, Portia labiata chose multi-minute roundabout paths — losing sight of prey spiders entirely — to reach an optimal attack position, satisfying the criteria for detour planning: prospective representation of a goal not currently visible.

In a 2005 PNAS study by Michael Krutzen, Janet Mann, and Richard Connor, Shark Bay dolphins were shown to wear marine sponges on their beaks to protect them while foraging on the rough seafloor; mitochondrial DNA showed the skill passes almost exclusively from mothers to daughters within one matriline, the first documented case of material tool-use culture in a marine mammal.

In Laguna, Brazil, wild bottlenose dolphins herd mullet toward cast-net fishermen and signal when to throw; a 2023 PNAS study by Mauricio Cantor, Damien Farine, and Fabio Daura-Jorge used drones and sonar to show 86 percent of catches came from synchronized dolphin-human interactions that benefit both species, formalizing a partnership first described by Karen Pryor in 1990.

In a 1991 Canadian Journal of Zoology study, John Ford showed that resident killer whale pods off British Columbia each produce 7 to 17 distinct call types grouped into four acoustic 'clans', dialects that persisted over 25 years and are learned by calves rather than inherited genetically.

In a 2012 Marine Mammal Science study, Robert Pitman and John Durban documented Antarctic pack-ice killer whales diving in synchrony to create coordinated bow waves that wash Weddell seals off ice floes, averaging four waves per hunt and overwhelmingly targeting that one seal species.

In a 2011 study in Behaviour, David Wiley and colleagues used suction-cup digital tags to reveal the underwater mechanics of cooperative humpback bubble-net feeding, identifying upward-spiral and double-loop swim paths the whales use to build cylindrical bubble curtains that corral fish, with all tagged whales feeding alongside partners.

In a 2011 Current Biology study, Ellen Garland and Michael Noad tracked 11 humpback song types spreading almost exclusively west-to-east across the South Pacific, from Australia through Tonga to French Polynesia, the first documented population-wide cultural transmission at an ocean-basin scale outside humans.

In their 1971 Science paper 'Songs of Humpback Whales', Roger Payne and Scott McVay showed the whales produce structured songs lasting 7 to 30 minutes built from a nested hierarchy of units, phrases, and themes, the discovery that revealed cetacean vocal complexity.

In a 2003 Proceedings of the Royal Society B study, Luke Rendell and Hal Whitehead showed that sperm whale groups in the Eastern Tropical Pacific belong to distinct 'vocal clans', each sharing a repertoire of Morse-like click patterns called codas that are culturally transmitted rather than inherited.

In a 2013 Journal of Comparative Psychology study, Peter Cook and Colleen Reichmuth at UC Santa Cruz showed Ronan, a California sea lion, could bob her head precisely in time to a musical beat and transfer the skill to novel tempos and songs, the first clear case of beat-keeping in a non-human mammal that lacks vocal mimicry.

subject_name: new caledonian crow aesop water task
hook: Jelbert et al. (2014, PLOS ONE) showed crows preferentially dropped sinking vs. floating objects and solid vs. hollow objects into water tubes to raise a floating reward, matching causal understanding of a 5-7 year-old child

Taylor, Hunt et al. (2007, Current Biology 17:1504-1507) showed 4 of 7 crows spontaneously used a short stick to extract a longer stick, then used the longer stick to reach food — first non-human metatool demonstration

subject_name: new caledonian crow compound tool assembly
hook: Bockmühl, Jelbert, Taylor, von Bayern et al. (Scientific Reports 2018) found 4 of 8 naïve crows spontaneously combined two short pipe segments into a longer functional tool to reach food; one bird 'Mango' assembled up to four parts

Bird & Emery (2009, Current Biology) gave 4 captive rooks stones and a cylinder with a floating worm; all 4 solved it, using exactly enough stones and preferring larger stones — notable because rooks don't use tools in the wild
Bird & Emery (PNAS 2009, 106:10370-10375) found all 4 rooks spontaneously bent wire into a hook to retrieve a bucket of food, 3 succeeding on first trial — a species with no wild tool use

Seed, Clayton & Emery (Proc Roy Soc B 2008, 275:1421) showed untrained rook pairs simultaneously pulled both ends of a string to bring in a food platform; success correlated with pair social tolerance

Bugnyar, Reber & Buckner (Proc Roy Soc B 2016 / earlier 2010 paper) showed ravens adjust caching behaviour based on whether competitors witnessed events; they re-cached when a conspecific was present but not when competitors were absent

subject_name: raven visual perspective taking unseen competitor
hook: Bugnyar, Reber & Buckner (Nature Communications 2016, 10506) demonstrated ravens hide food more cautiously when a peephole in a partition is open — even if no competitor is seen — implying they attribute visual access to unseen others

subject_name: raven future planning tool-use and bartering
hook: Kabadayi & Osvath (Science 2017, 357:202) trained ravens to use a stone tool to open a reward box, then tested them up to 17 hours later; ravens chose the correct tool over attractive distractors at ape-level performance

Marzluff et al. (2008, Animal Behaviour; follow-up 2010) showed wild American crows remembered a threatening rubber mask face for at least 2.7 years, scolding wearers in crowds and teaching the response to other crows

Prior, Schwarz & Güntürkün (PLOS Biology 2008, e202) used coloured marks on the neck of European magpies; 5 of 11 birds with visible marks directed scratching at the mark only when a mirror was present, the first non-mammal to pass

Clayton & Dickinson (Nature 1998, 395:272) showed western scrub jays remember which food (wax worm vs. peanut) they cached, where, and how long ago — the first non-human 'what-where-when' episodic-like memory demonstration

subject_name: scrub jay future planning for tomorrow
hook: Raby, Alexis, Dickinson & Clayton (Nature 2007, 445:919) showed jays preferentially cached food in a compartment where they had previously gone hungry, planning for future need independent of current hunger state

subject_name: jackdaw human gaze reading food retrieval
hook: von Bayern & Emery (Current Biology 2009) found hand-raised jackdaws took significantly longer to retrieve food when an unfamiliar human directed their eyes toward it than away; birds also used gaze alternation cues to find hidden food

Ostojić, Shaw, Cheke & Clayton (PNAS 2013, 110:4123) showed male Eurasian jays fed their female partners whichever food the female had not recently been pre-fed, appropriately tracking partner preference without being hungry themselves

Pepperberg (J Comparative Psychology 2006, 120:1) documented Alex the African grey spontaneously used the label 'none' to indicate an absent quantity during counting tasks — first bird to demonstrate a zero-like concept

Pepperberg (J Comparative Psychology 2006) showed Alex correctly answered 'how many?' for two sequentially presented sets of up to 6 objects, accurately producing the sum — numerical addition comparable to non-human primates

subject_name: alex african grey referential vocal labeling
hook: Pepperberg (decades of work, landmark 1987 & 1990 J Comparative Psychology papers) showed Alex functionally and referentially labelled >100 objects by color, shape, and material using English words, and could answer 'what's different?'

Patel, Iversen, Bregman & Schulz (Current Biology 2009, 19:827) showed Snowball the Eleonora cockatoo spontaneously adjusted dance movements to match tempo changes across six speeds of 'Everybody' by the Backstreet Boys — no food reinforcement

Auersperg, Szabo, von Bayern & Kacelnik (Current Biology 2012, 22:R903) documented Figaro the Goffin's cockatoo spontaneously biting, tearing and shaping splinters of wood into elongated tools to rake food into reach — novel species for bird tool manufacture

subject_name: goffin cockatoo five-step sequential lock task
hook: Auersperg, Kacelnik & von Bayern (PLOS ONE 2013, e68979) had 10 Goffin's cockatoos solve a box with 5 interlocked devices (pin, screw, bolt, wheel, latch); one naïve bird solved all five sequentially without demonstration

Auersperg, von Bayern, Gajdon, Huber & Kacelnik (PLOS ONE 2011, e20231) compared kea and New Caledonian crows on a box openable 4 ways; kea discovered 2-3 solutions in the first 10 trials and switched approaches faster when blocked

In a 2010 PLoS ONE study by Lucy King, Fritz Vollrath, and Iain Douglas-Hamilton (Oxford / Save the Elephants), playbacks of disturbed African honeybee sounds caused wild elephants to flee and emit a distinctive low-frequency rumble; when that rumble was replayed to other elephants, they fled faster and farther than during control rumble playbacks — the first documented referential alarm call in elephants for an insect threat.

In a 2014 PNAS study by Karen McComb and Graeme Shannon (University of Sussex), 47 wild elephant groups in Amboseli National Park correctly identified Maasai male voices as more dangerous than Kamba male voices — distinguishing ethnicity, gender, and age from voice alone in playback experiments, retreating and scent-checking with raised trunks only for the higher-threat voices.

In a 2007 Current Biology study by Alexandria Foote and Jonathon Crystal (University of Georgia), rats were offered the chance to skip an auditory duration test in exchange for a smaller guaranteed reward; they declined difficult trials more often and performed worse when forced to take them — the first demonstration of metacognitive uncertainty monitoring in a non-primate.

In a 2014 Nature Neuroscience study by Adam Steiner and A. David Redish (University of Minnesota), rats that passed a food option and then encountered a long wait at the next 'restaurant' looked back at the missed option and showed orbitofrontal cortex activity representing the skipped choice — not the missed food. Orbitofrontal neurons encoded the counterfactual action, matching the neural signature of regret in humans.

In a 2011 Science study by Inbal Ben-Ami Bartal, Jean Decety, and Peggy Mason (University of Chicago), free-roaming rats learned to open a restrainer door to release a trapped cagemate — without food reward and even when social contact was blocked afterward. When a chocolate restrainer was added, rats opened both and typically shared the chocolate, prioritising rescue over self-interest.

Tuttle and Ryan (1981, Science) showed that the fringe-lipped bat Trachops cirrhosus hunts tungara frogs by homing in on the males' mating calls in complete darkness, correctly distinguishing edible from poisonous species by call structure alone — the first documented case of a predator exploiting the acoustic communication channel of its prey to assess palatability before striking.

In a 2006 Science study by Alex Thornton and Katherine McAuliffe (Cambridge / Kalahari Meerkat Project), adult helpers at the Kuruman River Reserve modified their prey-delivery to pups based on each pup's begging call — removing scorpion stingers for the youngest pups, disabling (but not killing) scorpions for intermediate-aged pups, and delivering live intact scorpions to older pups — satisfying all three formal criteria for teaching in a non-primate.

In a 2006 PNAS study by Joshua Plotnik, Frans de Waal, and Diana Reiss (Bronx Zoo), three Asian elephants were exposed to a large mirror; one individual, Happy, repeatedly touched a painted white X above her eye while looking at her reflection — passing the gold-standard mark test and making elephants the third non-human taxon (after great apes and dolphins) confirmed to pass it.

In a 2016 Oxford study led by Cait Newport (published in Scientific Reports), archerfish (Toxotes chatareus) were trained to spit at one target face from a lineup of up to 44 human faces, reaching 81–86% accuracy — even when head shape and colour were stripped out, ruling out simple feature matching.

In 2011, Culum Brown and colleagues at Macquarie University published footage (Coral Reefs) of a wild blackspot tuskfish (Choerodon schoenleinii) repeatedly smashing a cockle against an anvil rock until it cracked open — the first documented tool use by a fish in the wild, with a pile of spent shells at the same rock suggesting habitual site use.

In a 2006 PLOS Biology study by Redouan Bshary and colleagues (University of Neuchâtel) at Ras Mohammed, Red Sea, coral groupers (Plectropomus pessuliferus) actively recruited giant moray eels via a rapid head-shake signal, then hunted cooperatively — the grouper flushing prey into open water while the eel pursued them into crevices, raising success for both.

Lester Aronson's landmark 1951/1971 experiments showed that frillfin gobies (Bathygobius soporator) allowed to swim over a tidal flat at high tide could accurately leap to adjacent pools at low tide — blind, without visual contact — achieving 97% success, demonstrating a cognitive map formed from a single high-tide survey.

In a 2007 Nature study by Logan Grosenick, Tricia Clement, and Russell Fernald at Stanford, male Astatotilapia burtoni cichlids watched dominance fights between strangers and correctly inferred the rank order of rivals they had never directly encountered — the first experimental demonstration of transitive inference in a fish.

Vladimir Dinets (University of Tennessee, 2013, Ethology Ecology & Evolution) observed American alligators and mugger crocodiles balancing sticks on their snouts near heron rookeries — luring nesting birds within strike range. Crucially, the behavior appeared only during breeding season when birds were actively collecting sticks, the first known case of tool use timed to a prey's seasonal behavior.

On November 4, 1960, Jane Goodall observed a chimpanzee she named David Greybeard at Gombe Stream, Tanzania stripping leaves from a grass stem and inserting it into a termite mound to extract termites — the first documented observation of tool manufacture by a non-human animal in the wild, prompting Louis Leakey to cable: 'Now we must redefine tool, redefine Man, or accept chimpanzees as humans.'

In a 2007 Current Biology paper by Sana Inoue and Tetsuro Matsuzawa at Kyoto University's Primate Research Institute, a young male chimpanzee named Ayumu memorized the locations of digits 1–9 flashed on a touchscreen for 210 milliseconds and then masked — outperforming all untrained human adults on this masked-numeral working-memory task.

In a 1985 Nature paper, Tetsuro Matsuzawa at Kyoto University's Primate Research Institute reported that a female chimpanzee named Ai — trained on a touchscreen since 1978 — used Arabic numerals 1 through 6 to correctly label exact quantities of objects, the first chimpanzee documented to use numerical symbols to represent set size in a peer-reviewed study.

In a 1993 controlled test by Sue Savage-Rumbaugh at Georgia State University's Language Research Center, bonobo Kanzi correctly responded to 74% of 660 novel spoken English commands — edging out a 2-year-old human child at 65% — having learned lexigrams incidentally as an infant by watching his mother's lessons rather than through direct training.

subject_name: chimpanzee inequity rejection brosnan de waal
hook: In a 2003 Nature paper, Sarah Brosnan and Frans de Waal demonstrated that capuchin monkeys paid a token for a cucumber slice rejected the food at high rates when they saw a partner receive a grape for the same task; Brosnan subsequently replicated the effect in chimpanzees — the first experimental evidence that non-human primates actively protest unequal pay for equal work.

Researcher Mathias Osvath at Furuvik Zoo, Sweden, documented male chimpanzee Santino calmly collecting stones and manufacturing concrete discs before zoo opening across five consecutive mornings, then hurling them at visitors during afternoon displays — published in Current Biology (2009) as the first clear evidence of spontaneous future-oriented planning for an emotional state hours away in a non-human.

Christophe Boesch's long-term field study at Taï National Park, Côte d'Ivoire, documented chimpanzee hunters taking specific non-overlapping roles — driver, blocker, chaser, ambusher — when pursuing red colobus monkeys, with group-hunt success at 63–89% versus 16% for solo hunters; published in Animal Behaviour (1994), this is the most elaborately role-differentiated cooperative hunt documented in a non-human species.

Jill Pruetz of Iowa State University and Paco Bertolani of Cambridge reported in Current Biology (2007) that savanna chimpanzees at Fongoli, Senegal, routinely broke branches, stripped bark and leaves, and sharpened tips with their teeth to form spears, then used them to stab sleeping bushbabies inside tree cavities — the first non-human animal documented systematically manufacturing and wielding a thrusting weapon to hunt vertebrates.

subject_name: chimpanzee bossou nut cracking cultural transmission
hook: A 16-year longitudinal study by Tetsuro Matsuzawa and colleagues at Bossou, Guinea, documented chimpanzees cracking oil-palm nuts with a stone hammer on a stone anvil, absent in adjacent communities with identical nut availability, and showed juveniles learn this during a critical window between ages 3 and 5 through observation — meeting all criteria for culturally transmitted technology.

A 1999 Nature paper by Andrew Whiten and colleagues synthesized 151 combined years of observation from seven African field sites and identified 39 behavioral patterns customary in some communities but absent in others with identical ecology — the most extensive documentation of cultural diversity in any non-human species, and the study that established the field of cultural primatology.

Gordon Gallup Jr.'s 1970 Science paper marked four wild-caught chimpanzees with red dye while anesthetized, then exposed them to mirrors; the chimps touched the dye marks on their own faces — not the reflection — establishing the mark test as the standard assay of animal self-awareness, and confirming that chimpanzees (and orangutans) recognize themselves in mirrors while gorillas tested in the same paradigm did not.

In 1953 on Koshima Island, a juvenile female macaque named Imo began washing sand off sweet potatoes in a stream—a behavior never seen before in the troop. Primatologist Masao Kawai documented in a 1965 Primates paper how the habit spread to Imo's playmates, siblings, and mother, establishing the first documented case of cultural transmission in a non-human primate.

In a 1980 Science paper, Robert Seyfarth, Dorothy Cheney, and Peter Marler played hidden tape-recorded alarm calls to free-ranging vervets at Amboseli, Kenya. Eagle alarms caused monkeys to look up; leopard alarms sent them into trees; snake alarms sent them looking at the ground—each response appropriate to the predator named, even in its absence. The study provided the first experimental evidence that a non-human animal uses referential signals to designate specific external dangers.

In a 2003 Nature study (volume 425, pp. 297–299), Sarah Brosnan and Frans de Waal showed that female capuchins given cucumber slices rejected the reward and sometimes threw it back when they watched a partner receive the more desirable grape for the same token-exchange task—the first experimental evidence of inequity aversion in a non-human animal.

In a 1998 Science paper (vol. 282, pp. 746–748), Elizabeth Brannon and Herbert Terrace trained two rhesus macaques to tap numerosities 1–4 in ascending order using varied shapes, sizes, and colors. When tested on novel numerosities 5–9 without any additional training, both monkeys immediately ordered the new values correctly, demonstrating an abstract ordinal concept of number rather than mere memorization.

In a 2013 Current Biology study, Daniel Takahashi and Asif Ghazanfar at Princeton University recorded marmosets in spontaneous vocal exchanges lasting up to 30 minutes. Each individual waited approximately 5 seconds after a partner finished calling before responding—mirroring human conversational turn-taking and unlike the chorusing seen in other non-human primates. The researchers modeled the exchanges as coupled oscillators, showing the timing was actively regulated rather than innate.

Joan Silk and colleagues published two landmark studies—Science 2003 (vol. 302, pp. 1231–1234) and Current Biology 2010—combining 16 years of behavioral data from wild Amboseli baboons. Females who formed strong, stable, equitable grooming partnerships had higher infant survival and lived significantly longer, independently of dominance rank. The finding was the first to quantitatively demonstrate that social bonds have direct fitness consequences in a non-human primate.

In a 2003 Proceedings of the Royal Society B study, Marc Hauser, M. Keith Chen, Frances Chen, and Emmeline Chuang tested genetically unrelated cotton-top tamarins in a food-giving apparatus. Tamarins preferentially gave food to individuals who had previously given food altruistically, but withheld food from those who had acted selfishly—the first experimental demonstration of reciprocally mediated altruism in a New World primate.

Tiago Falótico of the University of São Paulo led a 2019 Nature Ecology & Evolution study excavating a capuchin nut-cracking site at Serra da Capivara National Park, Brazil, unearthing quartz hammer stones radiocarbon-dated to 3,000 years ago—the oldest known non-human primate tool site outside Africa. The excavation also revealed that tool weight and striking strategy changed significantly around 2,400 years ago, suggesting the technology evolved within the population over millennia.

In 2007, satellite-tracked female E7 flew 11,680 km nonstop from Alaska to New Zealand in just over 8 days — the longest known nonstop migratory flight by any animal, documented by Robert Gill Jr. (USGS) and Phil Battley (Massey University) and published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B (2009).

In a 2005 Science paper from the University of Washington, Christopher Templeton and Erick Greene showed that the number of 'dee' notes at the end of the 'chick-a-dee' mobbing call encodes predator threat: small, agile raptors (e.g., pygmy owls) trigger more 'dee' notes than large, slow ones. Playback experiments confirmed other chickadees decode this information and mob accordingly.

In a 2016 Nature Communications study, Toshitaka Suzuki (Kyoto University) showed that Japanese tits combine an 'ABC' alarm call with a 'D' recruitment call into 'ABC-D' sequences that mean 'scan AND approach' — a meaning distinct from either call alone. Reversing the order to 'D-ABC' disrupts the behavior: birds rarely comply, demonstrating that syntactic order matters, the first experimental evidence for compositional syntax in a non-human animal.

In a 2012 Science study, Laura Kelley and John Endler (Deakin University) found that male great bowerbirds arrange objects in their bower courtyard in a size gradient — small objects nearest the display area, large ones at the far end — creating a forced perspective illusion that makes the courtyard appear uniformly sized to watching females. Males with stronger, more consistent illusions achieved higher mating success; when objects were experimentally scrambled, males restored the gradient within 3 days.

In a 2016 Science study, Claire Spottiswoode (Cambridge/Cape Town) showed that greater honeyguides in northern Mozambique respond specifically to the traditional Yao honey-hunters' call ('brrr-hm'), doubling the likelihood of being guided to a beehive from 33% to 66%, and tripling the overall success of locating hives. This is the only documented case of a wild, undomesticated animal and humans using mutually-understood referential signals to cooperate.

In a landmark 1988 Science paper, James Bednarz documented Harris's hawks hunting in coordinated parties of 2–6 using relay attack tactics: birds take turns as lead chaser to prevent prey escaping into cover, sustaining pursuit beyond any individual's ability. Cooperative hunting increased capture success and allowed the group to take prey larger than a single hawk could handle — one of the most rigorously documented cases of coordinated raptor group hunting.

In a 1978 Science paper, Eric Knudsen and Masakazu Konishi (Caltech) discovered the first neural map of auditory space in the barn owl midbrain: a 2D array of neurons encoding both horizontal and vertical sound-source location, made possible by the owl's vertically asymmetric ear openings. The map is experience-dependent and recalibrated by visual input — a foundational discovery in sensory neuroscience.

subject_name: egyptian vulture ostrich egg stone tool
hook: In 1966, Jane van Lawick-Goodall and Hugo van Lawick-Goodall documented in Nature the first scientific report of Egyptian vultures picking up rounded stones in their bill and striking ostrich eggs 4–12 times to breach the shell — one of the earliest published observations of spontaneous tool use in a wild bird. A 1989 Ibis study by Thouless et al. showed naïve captive birds developed the behavior through individual learning and strongly preferred rounded, egg-shaped stones.

Clark's nutcrackers store up to 33,000 pine seeds in ~5,000 scattered caches across several square kilometers each autumn, and recover enough of them through winter and spring to survive and feed nestlings — all from spatial memory alone. Studies by David Sherry and colleagues demonstrated that nutcracker hippocampus volume is proportionally larger than in non-caching corvids and that performance on cache-recovery tasks far exceeds what chance would predict.

In a 2018 RMIT study by Scarlett Howard and colleagues published in Science, individual honeybees trained on 'less than' rules subsequently placed an empty set (zero elements) below any non-zero numerosity — the first insect demonstrated to place zero on a numerical continuum, a feat previously seen only in primates and one African grey parrot.

In a 2019 RMIT study by Scarlett Howard, Aurore Avarguès-Weber, and colleagues published in Science Advances, free-flying honeybees learned that blue shapes meant 'add one' and yellow meant 'subtract one', then successfully applied those symbolic rules to novel quantities — the first demonstration of arithmetic using symbols in an invertebrate.

In a 2001 study by Martin Giurfa and colleagues published in Nature, honeybees learned abstract 'sameness' and 'difference' rules from visual stimuli in a delayed matching-to-sample task, then transferred those rules spontaneously to novel olfactory stimuli, demonstrating cross-modal abstract concept learning in an insect with under one million neurons.

In a 2022 Queen Mary University study by Samadi Galpayage and colleagues published in Animal Behaviour, 45 individually marked bumblebees rolled small wooden balls repeatedly even when no food reward was available; younger bees rolled more than older ones and males for longer than females — the first experimental demonstration of object play in any insect.

In a 2017 Science study by Olli Loukola, Clint Perry, and Lars Chittka, naive bumblebees that watched a trained demonstrator roll a ball to a target not only learned the task faster than unobserving controls but spontaneously adopted a more efficient technique than their tutor — the first evidence of social learning improving upon an observed solution in an insect.

In a 2024 Nature study by Alice Bridges, Lars Chittka, and colleagues, bumblebees individually could not solve a two-step puzzle box (push blue tab, then red tab) but readily learned the full sequence by watching a trained demonstrator; the behavior then spread culturally through naive colonies under open-diffusion conditions — the first cumulative-culture-like transmission documented in any invertebrate.

In a June 2026 Science study by Akshaye Bhambore, Olli Loukola, and colleagues at the University of Oulu, naive bumblebees that had separately learned a ball could be moved and that a blue flower held a reward spontaneously combined those two isolated memories to use the ball as a tool — the first demonstration of insight-like spontaneous problem-solving in any invertebrate.

In a 2006 Nature study by Nigel Franks and Tom Richardson at the University of Bristol, Temnothorax albipennis ants taught nest-mates routes to food via tandem running with bidirectional feedback: the leader slows when the pupil falls behind and resumes only after antennal contact — meeting the strict four-criteria definition of teaching, and the first time teaching was documented in any invertebrate.

Atta and Acromyrmex leafcutter ants have cultivated monocultures of the fungus Leucoagaricus gongylophorus for an estimated 8-12 million years, cutting vegetation solely as substrate and applying antibiotic-producing Streptomyces bacteria to suppress the parasitic fungus Escovopsis — a three-partner agricultural mutualism managed at colony scale with no individual aware of the whole system.

In a 2011 PNAS study by Nathan Mlot, Craig Tovey, and David Hu at Georgia Tech, Solenopsis invicta fire ants self-assembled into waterproof floating rafts within two minutes of flooding; by interlocking legs and bodies they trap air bubbles that reduce raft density by 75%, enabling colonies to float for weeks with no central coordinator and the queen automatically protected at the raft center.

In a 2002 Proceedings of the Royal Society B paper by Elizabeth Tibbetts, Polistes fuscatus wasps were shown to carry uniquely variable facial markings that function as identity signals; colony members recognize and respond differently to specific individual faces, while the close relative P. metricus which lacks this variation shows no such recognition — the first insect shown to use face signals for individual identity in a natural social context.

In a 2013 Current Biology study by Marie Dacke, Marcus Byrne, and colleagues at Lund University, Scarabaeus satyrus dung beetles tested in a Johannesburg planetarium oriented in straight lines under the full projected sky but wandered when only isolated stars were visible; the Milky Way band alone was sufficient for orientation — making dung beetles the first animal documented to navigate by the galaxy rather than individual stars.

In a 2020 Biology Letters study by McElligott, O'Keeffe, and Green (City University of Hong Kong / University of Roehampton), 10 of 11 captive but undomesticated kangaroos gazed directly at a human experimenter when faced with an unsolvable food box, and 9 of 11 alternated gaze between the box and the person — a referential communicative request previously thought to require domestication.

Charlton, Ellis, Brumm, and Fitch (University of Vienna / University of Queensland; PLOS ONE, 2011) showed via habituation-discrimination playback that both male and female koalas dishabituated significantly when an unfamiliar individual's bellow replaced a familiar one — the first experimental demonstration of individual vocal recognition in a marsupial.

Scheich, Langner, Tidemann, Coles, and Guppy (Nature, 1986) confirmed the platypus bill is a passive electroreceptive organ sensitive to electric fields as weak as ~50 µV/cm generated by the muscle contractions of prey — while the animal's eyes, ears, and nostrils are sealed shut during dives, making electroreception its primary active sensory channel. This was the first electroreception reported in any mammal.

Siegel, Manger, Nienhuis, Fahringer, Shalita, and Pettigrew (UCLA / University of Queensland; Neuroscience, 1999) found the platypus averages 5.8–8 hours of REM sleep per day — roughly 50% of total sleep time and far more than any other adult mammal studied — challenging the hypothesis that REM sleep reflects higher cortical processing, since the platypus cortex is comparatively simple.

Kendrick, da Costa, Leigh, Hinton, and Peirce at the Babraham Institute (Nature, November 2001) demonstrated that sheep can recognize and remember up to 50 individual sheep faces for over two years using right-hemisphere temporal and frontal lobe circuits analogous to human face-processing systems — the longest face memory retention window yet documented in a non-primate.

subject_name: California sea lion equivalence classes Kastak
hook: Schusterman and Kastak (UC Santa Cruz Long Marine Laboratory; Animal Behaviour, 1998) showed a California sea lion could form abstract stimulus equivalence classes — spontaneously transferring learned relationships between arbitrary symbols to untrained combinations and correctly applying a discriminative function to all class members in 28 of 30 novel tests, requiring conceptual grouping far beyond simple associative learning.

subject_name: Ronan the sea lion beat synchrony
hook: Cook, Rouse, Wilson, and Reichmuth (UC Santa Cruz Long Marine Laboratory; Journal of Comparative Psychology, 2013) demonstrated that a California sea lion named Ronan spontaneously synchronized head-bobbing to musical beats and generalized entrainment to novel tempos she had never heard — the first non-human mammal confirmed to exhibit true rhythmic entrainment, overturning the hypothesis that beat synchrony requires vocal mimicry circuitry.

Christine Harris and Caroline Prouvost (UC San Diego, 2014, PLOS ONE) tested 36 dogs at home: dogs snapped, pushed in, and touched a realistic stuffed dog toy when their owner showed it affection — significantly more than when owners interacted with a non-social object, the first experimental test of jealousy in a non-primate.

Friederike Range and colleagues at the University of Vienna (PNAS, 2009) showed that dogs tested in pairs stopped performing a paw-shake trick when the partner received a bread reward and they received nothing — demonstrating inequity aversion, a hallmark of fairness sensitivity previously thought primate-exclusive.

Jaroslav Červený and Hynek Burda (Czech University of Life Sciences / Univ. of Duisburg-Essen, Biology Letters, 2011) recorded 592 mousing pounces from 84 wild red foxes: jumps aimed northeast succeeded 73% of the time versus 18% in other directions, suggesting foxes use Earth's magnetic field as a distance-ranging system to judge prey position under snow.

subject_name: wolves do not look back miklosi 2003
hook: Miklósi, Kubinyi, Topál, Gácsi, Virányi, and Csányi (Eötvös Loránd University, Current Biology, 2003) placed socialized wolves and pet dogs in an unsolvable task: dogs consistently gazed back at the human experimenter for guidance; closely managed wolves did not — suggesting that reading humans as social partners is a uniquely domesticated trait.

Ueda, Kumagai, Yamaguchi, and Kohshima (Tokyo Institute of Technology / Kyoto University, PLOS ONE, 2014) found that gray wolves have high-contrast facial markings that highlight gaze direction and hold gazes significantly longer than other canids — evidence that within-pack gaze serves as a communication signal in a species that hunts cooperatively year-round.

Bradley Smith and Carla Litchfield (CQUniversity, Animal Cognition, 2013) presented dingoes with an unsolvable food-container problem: unlike domestic dogs, dingoes did not gaze back at human experimenters for help and instead persisted independently — revealing that human-directed social referencing is a domestication by-product absent in Australia's wild canid.

Marc Bekoff (University of Colorado, BioScience, 1974; ongoing Grand Teton field study) documented that coyotes use a stereotyped play-bow signal before and after actions that might be misread as aggressive, and self-handicap with weaker partners — a seven-year field study showed pups who played least had markedly higher dispersal mortality, linking social play to survival.

Erdohegyi, Topál, Virányi, and Miklósi (Eötvös Loránd University, Animal Behaviour, 2007) showed dogs can use exclusion logic — choosing the container NOT revealed to be empty — but only when no social-communicative cue was available from the experimenter; when a human gesture was present, dogs defaulted to that shortcut instead.

subject_name: dog helping trapped owner van bourg 2020
hook: Van Bourg, Patterson, and Wynne (Arizona State University, PLOS ONE, 2020) tested 60 pet dogs on releasing a trapped, visibly distressed owner from a box: dogs opened the box significantly more often when owners called for help versus when owners sat calmly inside reading aloud, demonstrating targeted prosocial helping behaviour toward familiar humans.

Kay Holekamp's lab (Michigan State University; Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2007) documented that spotted hyenas living in primate-like fission-fusion societies recognise third-party rank relationships and adjust coalition choices accordingly — social cognition comparable in complexity to cercopithecine primates, despite a carnivoran brain plan.

subject_name: spotted hyena vocal recognition cheney seyfarth
hook: Cheney, Seyfarth, and colleagues (University of Pennsylvania; in collaboration with Holekamp's lab, 2015) used playback experiments adapted from vervet monkey work to show wild spotted hyenas discriminate individual conspecifics by whoop vocalisations and use that information to coordinate long-distance coalition approach — the first such demonstration in a non-primate carnivoran.

Triana and Pasnak (Animal Learning & Behavior, 1981) tested two adult cats on invisible-displacement tasks — tracking an object moved unseen through sequential hiding places — and found performance consistent with Stage 6 object permanence, the same stage at which human infants begin full mental representation of absent objects.

Volker Deecke (University of Cumbria, Animal Cognition, 2012) photographically documented a wild Alaskan brown bear repeatedly picking up barnacle-encrusted rocks from the seafloor and using them to scratch its face during moulting — the first peer-reviewed record of tool use in a wild bear, with the animal selecting different rocks across three separate bouts.

Jennifer Vonk (Oakland University) and Michael Beran (Georgia State University, Animal Behaviour, 2012) trained three captive black bears on touchscreen numerosity-discrimination tasks; all three performed above chance across quantity comparisons, showing sensitivity to both absolute number and relative quantity — placing bears alongside primates in documented numerical cognition.

subject_name: african wild dog gps hunt hubel 2016
hook: Hubel, Myatt, Jordan, Dewhirst, McNutt, and Wilson (Royal Veterinary College / University of Birmingham / Botswana Predator Conservation Trust, Nature Communications, 2016) GPS-collared an entire wild dog pack at sub-second resolution and found hunts consisted of short individual sprints with opportunistic kills — no evidence of pre-planned role division, challenging popular accounts of wild dog 'coordinated strategy'.

Merola, Prato-Previde, and Marshall-Pescini (Animal Cognition, 2012) showed that dogs presented with an ambiguous novel object alternated their gaze between the object and their owner's face, and modulated approach or avoidance based on whether the owner expressed fear or happiness — the first controlled demonstration of genuine social referencing (emotional information-seeking from a human) in dogs.

Sarah Marshall-Pescini and colleagues at the Wolf Science Center Vienna (Scientific Reports, 2017) tested wolves and dogs on a loose-string cooperative pulling apparatus requiring two animals to pull simultaneously; wolves succeeded reliably while tolerant dog pairs also cooperated, but wolves showed proactive partner choice and initiated more joint attempts — evidence that cooperative tendencies predate domestication.

Deborah Custance and Jennifer Mayer (Goldsmiths, University of London, Learning & Behavior, 2012) had owners and strangers alternately hum or cry in front of their dogs: dogs oriented toward and approached the distressed person — whether familiar owner or unknown stranger — significantly more during crying than humming, suggesting dogs orient to distress cues rather than simply self-soothe or seek attention.

Gersick, Cheney, Schneider, Seyfarth, and Holekamp (Animal Behaviour, 2015) broadcast whoops from wild spotted hyenas at ranks higher or lower than the listener's own rank and found hyenas responded selectively in ways that tracked third-party dominance relationships — demonstrating recall of the social hierarchy across individuals beyond immediate rivals.

Brian Hare and colleagues (Harvard / Max Planck, multiple studies 2001–2010) showed that 9-week-old puppies with minimal human contact already follow distal pointing gestures to find hidden food — performing better than adult chimpanzees despite less experience — and that hand-reared wolves tested identically do not, identifying pointing comprehension as a domestication-selected cognitive adaptation.

Benson-Amram and Holekamp (Michigan State University, Animal Behaviour, 2012) tested 62 wild spotted hyenas on a novel metal puzzle box baited with meat: hyenas from large, complex social groups solved the box faster and more often than those from smaller groups — the first field-based test linking social group complexity to individual problem-solving performance in a carnivoran.

A 2024 PLOS ONE study using violation-of-expectancy methodology (measuring gaze duration at physically impossible outcomes) found that cats stared longer at scenes where a hidden object failed to reappear in its expected location, providing implicit evidence of object permanence that does not require the cat to physically search — sidestepping the motor-motivation confound of earlier displacement tasks.

In a 2017 paper in Marine and Freshwater Behaviour and Physiology, David Scheel (Alaska Pacific University) and colleagues documented a persistent den site — dubbed Octlantis — off Jervis Bay, Australia, where 10–15 Octopus tetricus occupied dens within metres of each other, engaged in mate guarding, den evictions, and repeated signalling interactions over eight observation days, overturning the assumption that octopuses are solitary.

subject_name: box jellyfish Tripedalia cystophora obstacle learning
hook: In a 2023 Current Biology paper by Bielecki, Dam Nielsen, Nachman, and Garm (Kiel University / University of Copenhagen), Caribbean box jellyfish (Tripedalia cystophora) were trained to avoid a grey-and-white striped tube simulating mangrove roots: after 7.5 minutes of pairing a visual cue with contact, they reduced collisions by 50% and increased turning rate — associative learning achieved with roughly 1,000 neurons and no centralised brain.

subject_name: mantis shrimp circularly polarized light signaling
hook: A 2015 Current Biology paper by Chiou, Cronin, Caldwell, and Marshall demonstrated that Gonodactylaceus falcatus reflects strongly circularly polarized light from its carapace, actively discriminates it, and uses it to avoid burrows occupied by conspecifics — a covert communication channel invisible to most other marine animals including cuttlefish and octopuses, which lack circular-polarization sensitivity.

subject_name: shore crab shock avoidance discrimination learning
hook: In a 2013 Journal of Experimental Biology paper by Robert Elwood and Mirjam Appel (Queen's University Belfast), shore crabs (Carcinus maenas) given mild electric shocks in one of two dark shelters learned over successive trials to choose the safe shelter, trading a preferred dark refuge for an aversive bright one to avoid future shocks — behaviour meeting a key criterion for pain-driven avoidance learning rather than nociceptive reflex.

subject_name: hermit crab shell pain trade-off Elwood
hook: In a 2009 Animal Behaviour paper by Robert Elwood and colleagues, hermit crabs (Pagurus bernhardus) given electric shocks inside their shells evacuated less readily when occupying a preferred high-quality shell than a less preferred one, showing a motivational trade-off between shock avoidance and shell value — evidence that their response was goal-directed rather than reflexive.

First described by Ivan Chase of Stony Brook University in 1986 and subsequently documented in multiple field and lab studies, hermit crabs form synchronous queues ranked by body size around a newly available shell: within seconds of the lead crab choosing the new shell, each crab in line shuffles into the shell vacated by the one ahead — a coordinated multi-individual social behaviour requiring assessment of relative shell and body size.

Jennifer Basil (Brooklyn College) and colleagues demonstrated classical conditioning in Nautilus pompilius using light as a conditioned stimulus paired with food: nautiluses learned the association rapidly and expressed temporally separated short-term memory (less than 1 hour) and long-term memory (6–24 hours post-training), a biphasic memory profile matching that of coleoid cephalopods despite the nautilus lacking the specialised brain lobes of its relatives.

A 2012 study published in Current Biology by Pignatelli and colleagues demonstrated that Sepia officinalis possesses the highest-acuity polarization vision yet measured in any animal, with spatial resolution for e-vector angle finer than that of mantis shrimp — used both for prey detection through water-column scatter and for reading polarized signals in conspecific communication, despite being completely colour-blind.

subject_name: mantis shrimp color temporal sampling Thoen Marshall
hook: A 2014 Science paper by Hanne Thoen, Martin How, Dán-Eric Nilsson, and Justin Marshall showed that despite 12 classes of photoreceptors, mantis shrimp (Haptosquilla trispinosa) performed poorly on wavelength discrimination tasks compared to humans — the 12 channels are not compared opponent-fashion but instead function as a rapid parallel colour-recognition system, labelling hues in under 25 milliseconds without fine discrimination.

subject_name: octopus active sleep skin patterning OIST 2023
hook: In a June 2023 Nature paper from the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology, researchers recording brain activity in sleeping Octopus laqueus found that quiet sleep phases were punctuated by approximately 60-second bouts of rapid chromatophore flickers, eye twitches, and arm contractions during which brain activity matched the waking state — an active sleep stage functionally analogous to mammalian REM sleep, suggesting offline neural processing in an invertebrate.

Roger Hanlon (Marine Biological Laboratory) observed a single Octopus cyanea foraging off Hawaii change its body pattern over 1,000 times during a 7-hour observation session — more than 150 pattern transitions per hour — each shift triggered by background substrate, suggesting continuous real-time perceptual matching rather than a fixed repertoire, and demonstrating active scene-reading as a cognitive process.

Roger Hanlon's group at the Marine Biological Laboratory showed through quantitative analysis of thousands of cuttlefish body-pattern images that Sepia officinalis operates a three-pattern decision tree — Uniform (flat background), Mottle (heterogeneous substrate), and Disruptive (high-contrast edges) — selected within 1–2 seconds of encountering a new substrate, implying fast visual scene categorization driving rapid motor output across millions of independently controlled chromatophores.

A January 2026 PNAS paper showed that Sepia officinalis males produce spatially patterned polarization signals during courtship that arise from birefringent muscle tissue in their arm skin, creating horizontal and vertical polarization bands at angles that maximise contrast for the cuttlefish's own polarization visual system — a channel invisible to humans and to most co-occurring predators.

subject_name: Portia fimbriata stalking detour over tree trunk
hook: Robert Jackson (University of Canterbury) documented in field and laboratory work that Portia fimbriata, when facing a web-shaking orb-weaver prey too dangerous to approach directly, routinely navigated completely out of sight of the target — circling a tree trunk, climbing above, then dropping on a silk line — with the chosen path consistently the route leading to the best attack angle, evidence of prospective goal-directed routing in a spider with a brain smaller than a sesame seed.

First described in 2001 by Norman, Finn, and Tregenza after nine mimic octopuses were filmed off North Sulawesi, Indonesia over two years, Thaumoctopus mimicus impersonates up to 13 locally co-occurring toxic or dangerous species — including flatfish, lionfish, and banded sea snakes — choosing postures that match each model's movement and silhouette, the only cephalopod species known to routinely deploy multiple functionally distinct mimicry targets.

In a 1992 PNAS study at Shark Bay, Richard Connor and colleagues documented male bottlenose dolphins forming nested 'second-order alliances' (alliances of alliances) of up to 14 males, the largest multi-level male cooperative network known outside humans.

In a 2013 Proceedings of the Royal Society B study, Stephanie King, Laela Sayigh, Vincent Janik and colleagues found bottlenose dolphins copy the signature whistles of close associates (mothers, calves, allied males) as a friendly addressing behavior, with copies slightly modified so they are not mistaken for deceptive mimicry.

At the Crozet Archipelago, killer whales deliberately strand on the beach to seize elephant seal pups; a 1995 Canadian Journal of Zoology study by Christophe Guinet and Joel Bouvier showed juveniles practice the risky technique from age 4 to 5 with adult females actively helping them back into the water, evidence of teaching.

In a 2015 Current Biology study, Lauren Brent, Darren Croft, and Ken Balcomb used 35 years of data to show post-reproductive female killer whales lead pod movements, especially in years when salmon are scarce, acting as repositories of ecological knowledge that helps explain the evolution of menopause.

In a 2017 Marine Mammal Science review, Robert Pitman of NOAA compiled 115 events spanning 62 years in which humpback whales actively interfered with mammal-eating killer whales, often defending other species such as seals; in 93 percent of approaches the orcas were the mammal-hunting ecotype, raising the possibility of interspecific altruism.

In a 2012 Current Biology paper, Sam Ridgway documented NOC, a beluga at the National Marine Mammal Foundation in San Diego, spontaneously over-inflating his vestibular sacs to produce speech-like sounds in a human register; the mimicry was so convincing a diver once surfaced asking who had told him to get 'out'.

Hoover, a harbor seal orphaned in Maine and raised at the New England Aquarium, mimicked human speech in a gruff New England accent, saying phrases like 'Hello there' and 'Get out of here'; his vocal mimicry was scientifically documented by Katherine Ralls and colleagues in a 1985 Canadian Journal of Zoology paper.

subject_name: new caledonian crow sequential three-tool problem
hook: Taylor, Elliffe, Hunt & Gray (2010, PLOS ONE e6471) tested crows on tasks requiring up to three sequential tools; subjects used tool 1 to retrieve tool 2, then tool 2 to retrieve tool 3, then tool 3 to reach food

subject_name: new caledonian crow hooked tool storage
hook: Klump, St Clair & Rutz (eLife 2021, e64829) showed crows more reliably stored hooked tools (complex to manufacture) underfoot or in holes between uses than basic non-hooked tools, indicating valuation-based tool care

subject_name: new caledonian crow causal analogical reasoning trap-table
hook: Taylor, Hunt, Holzhaider & Gray (2010, Communicative & Integrative Biology) found 3 crows that solved the trap-tube then spontaneously solved the causally equivalent but visually distinct trap-table, suggesting causal-analogical transfer

Bugnyar, Stöwe & Heinrich (Proc Roy Soc B 2004, 271:1331) showed hand-raised ravens consistently repositioned themselves to follow a human experimenter's gaze around a visual barrier, a capacity that emerged around 6 months of age

Bugnyar & Heinrich (2005, Animal Behaviour) showed ravens distinguish between knowledgeable and ignorant conspecific competitors when caching food, pilfering more from demonstrators who had witnessed caching events

subject_name: american crow danger learning from conspecific death
hook: Swift & Marzluff (Animal Behaviour 2015) showed wild crows formed an aversive association with a novel human face after a single event pairing that face with a dead crow, retaining the memory for at least 6 weeks

subject_name: jackdaw social learning danger from alarm calls
hook: Researchers (2019, Scientific Reports and related work) showed breeding jackdaws exposed to an unfamiliar human paired with conspecific alarm calls showed heightened fear responses in subsequent encounters with that person, demonstrating rapid social learning

subject_name: african grey parrot object permanence invisible displacement
hook: Pepperberg & Kozak (1986) and Pepperberg & Willner (1990, J Comparative Psychology) showed adult grey parrots successfully solved Piagetian Stage 6 invisible displacement tasks, outperforming most non-human primates on this benchmark

subject_name: african grey parrot number cardinal inference
hook: Pepperberg & Carey (Cognition 2012) showed Griffin, a young grey parrot, correctly labelled novel sets of 7 and 8 items on first trials before full training, inferring cardinal value from ordinal position in the numeral list

Schwing, Jocteur, Wein, Massen & Noë (Animal Cognition 2016) showed kea dyads solved a loose-string cooperation task; pairs with higher social affiliation cooperated more successfully, with birds attending to partner string-handling improving performance

subject_name: kea social learning problem solving Huber
hook: Huber, Rechberger & Taborsky (Animal Behaviour 2001) showed captive kea opened significantly more locks on a complex food box after observing a skilled demonstrator, with juvenile birds being most exploratory — social play drives innovation

subject_name: budgerigar contact call convergence vocal culture
hook: Farabaugh, Linzenbold & Dooling (Behaviour 1994) showed that adult male budgerigars housed together converged on shared contact call types within 8 weeks via mutual imitation, demonstrating adult vocal learning for social bonding

subject_name: new caledonian crow tool cultural traditions
hook: Hunt & Gray (Proc Roy Soc B 2003) and Kenward et al. (2006, Anim Behav) documented that distinct tool designs — basic, stepped, and hooked pandanus-leaf tools — persist across decades in different geographic regions, consistent with cultural transmission

Bogale, Kamata, Mioko & Sugita (Animal Cognition 2011) trained jungle crows to discriminate 2 vs. 5 items with non-numerical controls; birds transferred to novel pairs (5 vs. 8) showing true numerical discrimination not based on continuous magnitudes

Bugnyar, Stöwe & Heinrich (Proc Roy Soc B 2004, 271:1331) showed visual co-orientation with human gaze appears in raven fledglings, but gaze-following around barriers only emerges at ~6 months, suggesting a developmental trajectory for perspective-taking

subject_name: american crow funeral danger learning neural basis
hook: Iglesias, Weir & Marzluff (Behavioural Brain Research 2020) used implanted electrodes to show exposure to dead conspecifics activates the nidopallium caudolaterale (avian executive cortex analog) in American crows — linking social mortality response to higher cognition

subject_name: eurasian jay cache protection strategy distance
hook: Legg & Clayton (Animal Cognition 2014) showed Eurasian jays cached food at greater distances from an observing conspecific, and preferentially chose opaque over transparent barriers — active spatial strategy against pilfering

Pepperberg (Learning & Behavior 1987) demonstrated Alex correctly identified 'same' or 'different' across color, shape, and material — and transferred to novel object pairs — showing abstract categorical comparison without prior training on specific pairs

Osuna-Mascaró, Auersperg et al. (Scientific Reports 2022) showed Goffin's cockatoos spontaneously constructed composite tools by combining a short stick and a ball of clay to extend their reach — functional tool assembly from disparate materials

subject_name: new caledonian crow causal physical reasoning
hook: Taylor, Hunt, Holzhaider & Gray (Proc Roy Soc B 2009, 276:247) found crows in a trap-tube task avoided functional traps but not matched non-functional holes, suggesting they tracked causal structure rather than surface features

Cynthia O'Connell-Rodwell (Stanford/University of Nevada) found in field studies from 1992 onward that African elephants detect ground-borne infrasound vibrations through their feet and trunk tip, and can distinguish between seismic signals from familiar and unfamiliar herds — a 'caller ID' system that operates kilometres beyond airborne vocal range.

In a 2014 study by Joshua Plotnik and Frans de Waal (Emory University / Mahidol University), Asian elephants at a Thai sanctuary spontaneously approached distressed herd-mates, chirping softly and touching their faces and mouths with the trunk tip — the first empirical evidence of consolation behaviour in elephants, previously documented only in great apes, canines, and corvids.

In a 2011 PNAS study by Joshua Plotnik, Richard Lair, and Frans de Waal, 12 Asian elephants at the Thai Elephant Conservation Center learned to pull a rope in synchrony to slide a food table within reach; crucially, elephants waited up to 45 seconds for a delayed partner rather than pulling alone — demonstrating deliberate partner-awareness in a cooperative task previously used to test primates.

subject_name: authai the asian elephant numerical discrimination
hook: In a 2018 Journal of Ethology study by Naoko Irie and colleagues, a 14-year-old Asian elephant named Authai at Ueno Zoo used a touch-panel computer to select the larger of two dot arrays; her accuracy held steady even for numerosities above 4 and was unaffected by the ratio or magnitude of the pair — performance consistent with counting-like processes rather than the analogue magnitude system seen in most non-human animals.

In a 2013 Nature study by Brad Pfeiffer and David Foster (Johns Hopkins University), rat hippocampal place cells were recorded during rest pauses in an open arena; the cells replayed spatial sequences biased toward the current reward location, even on novel start-goal combinations the animal had never run — the first direct evidence that awake hippocampal replay projects future, not merely past, trajectories.

In a 2001 Neuron study by Kenway Louie and Matthew Wilson (MIT), multineuronal firing sequences that rats expressed during maze running were replayed during subsequent REM sleep at the same timescale — stretches up to 2 minutes long reproduced in real time, the first demonstration that episodic-like experience is consolidated in mammals during REM.

In a 2006 Science study by Dale Langford and Jeffrey Mogil (McGill University), mice co-housed with a cage-mate writhing in pain made significantly more writhing movements themselves when given a noxious stimulus, while mice paired with strangers showed no such amplification; the effect was abolished by blocking the field of view, establishing visual emotional contagion as the mechanism.

In a 2016 Science study by James Burkett, Elissar Andari, Zack Johnson, and Frans de Waal (Emory University), prairie voles whose cage partners had received a mild shock significantly increased partner-directed grooming, an effect blocked by an oxytocin antagonist and absent in asocial meadow voles — the first experimental evidence of consolation (empathy-motivated social buffering) in rodents.

Wild eastern gray squirrels observed and documented in studies including Leaver et al. (2007, Animal Behaviour) dig shallow cache holes and carefully tamp down the earth while keeping the food in their cheek pouches, producing a convincing decoy burial — a behaviour that occurred significantly more often when a conspecific observer was present but not when a corvid watched, indicating the deception is socially targeted.

subject_name: gray squirrel scatter hoard spatial memory
hook: Field studies by Lucia Jacobs and Emily Liman (UC Berkeley, 1991) demonstrated that gray squirrels could relocate individual cached sites using spatial memory alone — recovering seeds planted by the researchers at exactly the squirrel's own cache locations at rates far above chance, even after olfactory cues were masked, establishing spatial mapping as the primary retrieval mechanism.

subject_name: naked mole rat colony vocal dialect
hook: In a 2021 Science study by Alison Barker and colleagues (Max Planck Institute), analysis of over 36,000 soft-chirp greetings from 166 naked mole-rats in seven colonies revealed colony-specific dialects; cross-fostered pups adopted their adoptive colony's chirp, and the dialect deteriorated when a queen died but re-cohered under a new queen — the first demonstration of culturally transmitted vocal dialects in a rodent.

subject_name: fringe-lipped bat social learning novel prey call
hook: In a 2006 Current Biology study by Rachel Page and Michael Ryan (Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute), naive fringe-lipped bats that could observe a trained demonstrator learning to associate a novel artificial frog call with food acquired the association in a mean of 5.3 trials; bats learning alone rarely succeeded even after 100 trials — demonstrating rapid cultural transmission of foraging knowledge in a bat.

In a 2021 Frontiers in Psychology study by Candace Croney and colleagues (Purdue University), four pigs — two Yorkshire (Hamlet and Omelette) and two Panepinto micro-pigs (Ebony and Ivory) — operated a joystick with their snouts to move an on-screen cursor into targets, performing significantly above chance and maintaining the association even when food-dispenser malfunctions meant social praise was the only reward.

subject_name: pig mirror spatial awareness food location
hook: In a 2009 Animal Behaviour study by Donald Broom and colleagues (Cambridge University), pigs exposed to a mirror for 5 hours and then shown a food bowl visible only via its reflection used the mirror information to walk directly to the bowl — ruling out the alternative hypotheses that they followed scent or had seen the bowl directly; pigs tested without prior mirror exposure instead investigated behind the mirror.

In a 2016 Applied Animal Behaviour Science study by Cecilie Mejdell and colleagues (Norwegian Veterinary Institute), all 23 horses of varied breeds and ages were successfully trained in 10–15 min daily sessions to touch one of three symbols on a board — a horizontal bar for 'put blanket on', a vertical bar for 'take blanket off', and a blank for 'no change' — and made choices correlated with ambient temperature, indicating genuine preference communication.
